rules.quote: Choose words that people are familiar with.
rules.specification: Prefer familiar, everyday words over obscure or bureaucratic vocabulary.
rules.violation_condition: use of unfamiliar or overly complex bureaucratic words when familiar everyday alternatives exist
rules.why: G-4: The candidate heading is supported by the direct imperative sentence; examples directly contrast everyday words with legalese.

rules.violation_condition: use of a double negative construction in a sentence
rules.why: Explicit prohibition under Accessibility requirements fundamentals.

covers.quote: Use ‘we’, ‘you’ and ‘us’ if you can

parts.quote: We will assess your application within 30 days.

rules.quote: Use personal pronouns (like ‘we’, ‘you’, ‘us’) when it suits the voice and tone.
rules.specification: Use personal pronouns ('we', 'you', 'us') to maintain an active, engaging tone where suitable.
rules.violation_condition: avoidance of personal pronouns in favour of impersonal passive constructions when addressing users
when: When it suits the voice and tone.
rules.why: G-4: Heading consolidated into the body sentence stating the rule.

covers.quote: Avoid jargon
Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases, idioms and so on.

parts.quote: They changed their decision in response to new information.
They changed their decision in light of new information.

rules.specification: Do not use jargon, slang, or idioms in plain language content.
rules.violation_condition: presence of jargon, slang, or idiomatic expressions
rules.why: G-4: Heading and WCAG fundamental consolidated into the explicit rule statement.

covers.quote: Use inclusive language

rules.quote: Choose words that respect all people, including their rights and their heritage.
rules.specification: Use inclusive language that respects all people, their rights, and their heritage.
rules.violation_condition: use of non-inclusive language that fails to respect people, their rights, or their heritage
rules.why: G-4: Consolidated candidate heading into its defining body instruction.

covers.quote: Choose simple words, not complicated expressions
Don’t write this
Try this instead

rules.quote: Replace longer words and phrases with simpler alternatives.
rules.specification: Check text against the provided table of complicated expressions (e.g. 'acquire', 'additional', 'cease', 'utilise', 'whilst', etc.) and replace them with simpler words.
rules.violation_condition: use of a word or phrase from the complex expressions list (e.g. 'acquire', 'in order to', 'utilise', 'whilst') when a simpler alternative is available
when: Except when tabling a document in parliament for the verb 'table'.
rules.why: G-4: Heading absorbed into instruction introducing the lookup substitution table.

covers.quote: Be selective about shortened forms, such as abbreviations, contractions, acronyms and initialisms.
Try to avoid them altogether if they are used only once or twice.
In content with many specialist terms, reserve shortened forms for the most frequently used terms only. Spell out other terms in full.

rules.quote: Shorten only the words and phrases that are well known or used many times in your content.
rules.specification: Do not use shortened forms for terms that only appear once or twice, unless the shortened form is widely known.
rules.violation_condition: abbreviating words or phrases that are neither well known nor frequently used in the content
when: Shortened forms that are well known or listed in a dictionary (e.g. 'DNA') are permitted.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: Consolidated multiple restatements across the section on restricting acronyms/shortened forms.

covers.quote: Expand all acronyms on their first use.

examples.note: Shortened form spelled out on first use.

parts.quote: The Digital Transformation Agency (DTA) helps government agencies create digital services.

rules.quote: Spell them out the first time you use them.
rules.specification: When introducing an acronym or initialism, spell out the full term on first use, accompanied by the shortened form.
rules.violation_condition: using a shortened form (acronym or initialism) on first use without spelling out the full term
when: Unless the shortened form is better known than the full form (e.g. 'DNA').
rules.why: G-4: Restatement of the rule under Accessibility requirements; example directly illustrates this.
